Reciprocal scaling and cancellation at a pole

Exposition and figures by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Original exposition and exercises: CC0. Supplied programme prerequisites retain their stated licences.

A reciprocal tail can converge to a principal value when it is compressed toward the origin. An integrable perturbation leaves a point mass instead. We separate these two effects, express every derivative of a principal value by a convergent finite-difference integral, and calculate the point terms that survive cancellation of boundary poles.

All pairings are complex-linear. Write , , and The definition and complete boundary-limit proofs are Cauchy kernels and boundary limits, Section 4, Theorem 4.1 and Corollary 4.2: Here the boundary notation means the limit of with . The cited proof gives a uniform bound on tests supported in : In particular has order at most one. Its order is exactly one: its nonzero punctured restriction is homogeneous of degree , and Euler equations and the order of singularities, Lemma 4.1, proves by disjoint annular tests that an order extension must satisfy .

The same normalization gives The first identity is proved by the endpoint integration in Finite parts of singular powers, Proposition 5.1; the full logarithmic traces and their derivatives are Complex powers at a boundary, Theorem 4.1. Thus the real logarithm and its two boundary branches have distinct derivatives at the origin.

The test topology is Order, positivity and distributional limits, Section 1. The supplied scalar foundations, §§12–13, and integration foundations, §§15–16, prove cutoffs, Taylor estimates, Rolle's theorem, absolute integration, substitution and dominated convergence used below. The supplied finite algebra, §§10.3–10.4, proves rank-nullity and elimination, including the kernel and inverse criteria for square matrices.

Proof. We use the following elementary root count. A nonzero real linear combination of distinct nonnegative integer powers of has at most distinct positive zeros. For it has none. For , divide by its smallest power, without changing positive zeros. Differentiating removes the nonzero constant term and leaves a combination of distinct powers. If the original had distinct positive zeros, Rolle's theorem would give at least distinct positive zeros of that derivative, contradicting induction. The same argument excludes any larger number by selecting zeros.
